BASE self.camera.background_color = "#000000" self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP) self.add(self.title) # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-") lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines] self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8) self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2) self.add(self.lecture) # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side) self.grid = {} rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"] # Top to bottom cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"] # Left to right for i, row in enumerate(rows): for j, col in enumerate(cols): x = 0.5 + j * 1 y = 2.2 - i * 1 self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0]) def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0): mobject.scale(scale_factor) mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos]) return mobject def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0): tl_pos = self.grid[top_left] br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right] # Calculate center of the area center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2 center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2 center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0]) mobject.scale(scale_factor) mobject.move_to(center) return mobject class Section6Scene(TeachingScene): def construct(self): # Setup layout with specific title and lecture lines self.setup_layout( "Application: Solving Linear Systems", [ 'Systems of linear differential equations use this tool.', 'The solution is e to At times the initial state.', 'Matrix exponentials are the fundamental propagators of linear systems.' ] ) # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 === self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#FFFF00"), run_time=0.5) # Using Text instead of MathTex to avoid LaTeX dependency errors diff_eq = Text("dx/dt = Ax", font_size=32) initial_cond = Text("x(0)", color="#FFA500", font_size=28) # Positioning self.place_in_area(diff_eq, "A2", "B4") self.place_at_grid(initial_cond, "B5") # Fixed: closer to equation (Issue 48) self.play(FadeIn(diff_eq), FadeIn(initial_cond)) self.wait(1) # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 === self.play( self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(WHITE), self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#FFFF00"), run_time=0.5 ) # Create solution text using VGroup to allow targeted coloring/animation of specific parts sol_eq = VGroup( Text("x(t) = ", font_size=32), Text("e^At", font_size=32), Text(" x(0)", font_size=32) ).arrange(RIGHT, buff=0.1) # Fixed: Adjusted area to avoid propagator label collision (Issue 47) self.place_in_area(sol_eq, "C2", "C5", scale_factor=1.0) # Create propagator label propagator_label = Text("Propagator", font_size=24, color="#00FF00") self.place_at_grid(propagator_label, "D3") self.play(FadeIn(sol_eq)) # Flash the term e^At and show label self.play( sol_eq[1].animate.set_color("#00FF00"), Indicate(sol_eq[1], color="#00FF00"), Write(propagator_label) ) self.wait(1) # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 === self.play( self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(WHITE), self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#FFFF00"), run_time=0.5 ) # Define a vector field for the streamlines (stable spiral) def flow_func(p): x, y = p[:2] # Simple spiral sink dx/dt = -0.5x + y; dy/dt = -x - 0.5y return np.array([-0.5 * x + y, -x - 0.5 * y, 0]) # Create StreamLines object stream_lines = StreamLines( flow_func, x_range=[-2, 2], y_range=[-2, 2], stroke_width=2, color=BLUE_E, opacity=0.4 ) # Fixed: Reduced width and scale to avoid cramped appearance (Issue 49) self.place_in_area(stream_lines, "E2", "F5", scale_factor=0.5) # Add 5 dots to follow streamlines start_points = [ [1.5, 1.5, 0], [-1.5, 1.0, 0], [1.0, -1.5, 0], [-1.2, -1.2, 0], [0.5, 1.8, 0] ] dots = VGroup() for pt in start_points: dot = Dot(point=pt, color="#00FFFF", radius=0.06) dots.add(dot) # Scale and move dots group relative to stream_lines (Scale matches Issue 49) dots.scale(0.5) dots.move_to(stream_lines.get_center()) def update_dot(mob, dt): # Calculate direction relative to center of field relative_pos = (mob.get_center() - stream_lines.get_center()) / 0.5 v = flow_func(relative_pos) mob.shift(v * dt * 0.4) # Recycle dots if they get too close to center if np.linalg.norm(relative_pos) < 0.1: mob.move_to(stream_lines.get_center() + np.array([np.random.uniform(-1,1), np.random.uniform(-1,1), 0]) * 0.5) self.play(FadeIn(stream_lines)) self.add(dots) # Attach updaters for dot in dots: dot.add_updater(update_dot) self.wait(4) # Clean up updaters for dot in dots: dot.remove_updater(update_dot) # Final state color correction self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(WHITE), run_time=0.5) self.wait(1) # To render: manim -ql section_6.py Section6Scene

outline.topic: Matrix Exponentials: The Secret to System Evolution
outline.target_audience: University students in Linear Algebra or Differential Equations

sections.title: The Growth Analogy: From Scalars to Matrices
sections.content: Start with the familiar scalar growth equation dx/dt = rx, where the solution is x(t) = e^(rt). Introduce the concept of extending this to systems of variables represented by vectors. Use a split-screen animation showing a single 'growing' circle (scalar) next to a 'stretching and rotating' grid (matrix).
sections.example: A single colony of bacteria growing at a rate 'r' versus a complex ecosystem of two interacting species (predators and prey) whose populations depend on each other through a matrix 'A'.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Taylor Series Bridge
sections.content: Briefly revisit the Taylor Series for e^x. Explain that because we can add and multiply square matrices, we can plug a matrix into this power series. Visually show the summation terms 1 + x + x^2/2! + ... transforming into I + At + (At)^2/2! + ... with matrices visually stacking to form the final result.
sections.example: An animated 'Taylor Machine' where you feed in a scalar value to get a curve, then swap the input for a 2x2 matrix to see the components of the matrix evolve.

sections.title: The Formal Definition of e^(At)
sections.content: Define the matrix exponential e^(At) using the power series. Emphasize that 't' acts as a time scaling factor. Use a graphical representation of a coordinate plane where the basis vectors start to 'flow' along paths determined by the sum of these matrix powers.
sections.example: Imagine a 'Time-Travel Remote' where the button 't' smoothly warps a square grid into a skewed or rotated shape based on the instructions inside matrix A.

sections.title: The Computational Shortcut: Diagonalization
sections.content: Introduce the 'shortcut' for calculating e^(At) when matrix A is diagonalizable (A = PDP^-1). Explain that e^(At) = P * e^(Dt) * P^-1. Graphically show the process: 1. Change basis (P^-1), 2. Scale along axes (e^Dt), 3. Change back (P).
sections.example: A 'Robot Arm' (P) that re-orients a package so a simple 'Stretching Machine' (e^Dt) can work on it, before the arm rotates it back to the original orientation.

sections.title: Geometric Intuition: Rotations and Scaling
sections.content: Show what different types of matrices produce in the exponential. A skew-symmetric matrix leads to a rotation (e^At is an orthogonal matrix), while a diagonal matrix leads to pure scaling. Use an animation of a character 'Vector' traveling in circles or spiraling outward.
sections.example: A compass needle (Vector) spinning in a magnetic field represented by a skew-symmetric matrix, showing continuous rotation as time 't' advances.

sections.title: Application: Solving Linear Systems
sections.content: Connect the math to the ultimate goal: solving the differential equation dx/dt = Ax. The solution is x(t) = e^(At) * x(0). Highlight that the matrix exponential is the 'fundamental solution' that transitions the system from the initial state to any future state.
sections.example: A flight simulator where the joystick input (matrix A) determines how the plane's orientation (x) evolves over time (t) starting from a takeoff position (x0).

storyboard.title: The Growth Analogy: From Scalars to Matrices
lecture_lines: Simple growth follows the equation dx/dt equals rx.
The solution is the familiar exponential function, e to rt.
In systems, matrices replace scalars to describe multi-variable growth.
animations: Create Text 'dx/dt = rx' in #FFFFFF at center.
Transform Text to 'x(t) = x(0)e^{rt}'. Create a Circle (#00FFFF) that scales from radius 1 to 2.
Move equation and circle to left half. Create Text 'd\mathbf{x}/dt = A\mathbf{x}' in #00FFFF on right half.
Create a 2D CoordinateSystem on the right. Add Vector [1, 0] (#FF0000) and Vector [0, 1] (#00FF00).
Animate the CoordinateSystem applying a linear transformation over time t, with the vectors tracing their paths.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Taylor Series Bridge
lecture_lines: Recall the Taylor Series for e to the x.
We can sum powers of matrices just like numbers.
Replace the scalar x with the matrix product At.
Each term involves powers of the matrix A.
This series defines the exponential of a matrix.
animations: Create Text 'e^x = 1 + x + \frac{x^2}{2!} + \dots' in #FFFFFF. Highlight x in #FFD700.

Replace x with At to show 'e^{At} = I + At + \frac{(At)^2}{2!} + \dots' using [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/bridge.svg] to symbolize the conceptual bridge between scalar and matrix series. Highlight I in #00FFFF.
Show 3 distinct 2x2 Matrix objects (#FFFFFF) vertically stacked, with '+' signs between them, then merge them into a single Matrix labeled 'e^{At}'.

storyboard.title: The Formal Definition of e^(At)
lecture_lines: The matrix exponential e to At is a power series.
Identity plus At plus higher-order matrix powers.
Time 't' scales the evolution of the system.
Matrix powers warp the space over time.
This transforms initial states into future trajectories.
animations: Create Text 'e^{At} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{(At)^k}{k!}' in #FFFFFF.
Add a ValueTracker-controlled Slider at bottom labeled 't' (#FFFF00).
Create a NumberPlane with vectors i_hat (#FF0000) and j_hat (#00FF00).
As Slider moves, animate the vectors along curved trajectories.
Draw trailing curves behind the vector heads to show the path of evolution.

storyboard.title: The Computational Shortcut: Diagonalization
lecture_lines: Computing infinite series directly is often difficult.
Diagonalization simplifies the matrix A into P D P-inverse.
The exponential of a diagonal matrix is easy to compute.
Change basis, scale the components, then change back.
This shortcut makes matrix exponentials computationally practical.
animations: Create Text 'A = PDP^{-1}' with P in #FF00FF and D in #FFFF00.
Show the substitution into the series to get 'e^{At} = P e^{Dt} P^{-1}'.
Create a Vector (#FFFFFF) in a NumberPlane.
Animate the Vector rotating/scaling as P^{-1} is applied (aligning to eigenvectors).
Scale the Vector along the axes (diagonal growth), then apply P to rotate back.

storyboard.title: Geometric Intuition: Rotations and Scaling
lecture_lines: Diagonal matrices result in pure scaling along axes.
Skew-symmetric matrices create continuous rotations in space.
The exponential maps local rates to global transformations.
animations: Show Matrix A = [[1, 0], [0, 0.5]] and a unit Circle (#FFFFFF). Animate Circle stretching into an Ellipse.
Show Matrix A = [[0, -1], [1, 0]] and the unit Circle. Animate a Vector (#00FFFF) on the circle rotating.
Show the Vector's path as a circle, emphasizing that skew-symmetry leads to rotation.

storyboard.title: Application: Solving Linear Systems
lecture_lines: Systems of linear differential equations use this tool.
The solution is e to At times the initial state.
Matrix exponentials are the fundamental propagators of linear systems.
animations: Create Text 'd\mathbf{x}/dt = A\mathbf{x}' with 'x(0)' in #FFA500.
Create Text 'x(t) = e^{At}x(0)'. Flash the term 'e^{At}' in #00FF00 and label it 'Propagator'.
Create a StreamPlot (vector field) and animate 5 small Dots (#00FFFF) following the streamlines from different starting positions.
